fixes.explanation: Right, baker. The LORD says, “Do not leave any of it until morning…” The meal is for that night, so the deadline hits before breakfast. Whatever is left over has to be burned up before the morning comes. I've never kept a cookie past midnight in my life, so that rule would suit me fine.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “When you enter the land that the LORD will give you as He promised, you are to keep this service.” The LORD made a promise about a land, and Moses says the service goes with them into it. They haven't even left Egypt yet, and Moses is already giving instructions for the other side. That's planning ahead.

The LORD never says anything like that, friend. He says Pharaoh “…will allow you to leave this place.” Moses also tells Pharaoh that his officials will come and bow, saying, “Go, you and all the people who follow you!” (Exodus 11:8). Half a parade is just a sad walk down the road, so I'm glad that's not the plan.

Nothing about flocks being held back shows up in this promise. The LORD says Pharaoh will allow Israel to leave, and when he lets them go, he will drive them out completely. Picture getting driven out the door while the one doing the driving yells, “Wait, leave the sheep!” That doesn't fit the words the LORD gives.

Cattle and sheep sound like a reasonable ask, baker, but they aren't in this request. The LORD tells Moses that men and women alike should ask their neighbors for articles of silver and gold. Silver and gold are the two things He names, and livestock isn't one of them.

Right, baker. The text says Moses himself “…was highly regarded in Egypt by Pharaoh’s officials and by the people.” Think about that for a second. After all those wonders, Pharaoh's own officials still think highly of him. I'd be thrilled if a baker still thought that much of me after one burnt batch.

Lamps don't come up here, friend. The message says that among all the Israelites, “…not even a dog will snarl at man or beast.” A lamp is a fair guess for a midnight scene, since the LORD does say “About midnight” (Exodus 11:4). But the message names a dog and a snarl.

A creaking door is a fair guess, but it's not in the message. What it says is that among all the Israelites, “…not even a dog will snarl at man or beast.” The message gives a dog and a snarl, not a door and a creak.

Yes, baker. Moses tells Pharaoh his officials will come and bow before him, saying, “Go, you and all the people who follow you!” Those are Pharaoh's own officials in that picture, and they're the ones bowing. Then, the text says, Moses left Pharaoh's presence hot with anger.

Staying isn't what Moses says, friend. He says the officials will come and bow and say, “Go, you and all the people who follow you!” The word he gives them is go. Stay and keep working is the opposite of that.

No flock condition shows up in what Moses says. He says the officials will come and bow and say, “Go, you and all the people who follow you!” Not a word about flocks in that line. The words he gives them are go, and all the people who follow you.

You've got it, baker. The LORD says, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that My wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.” Moses and Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), did all the wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart anyway. The story keeps going.

You've got it, baker. The LORD says that if a household is too small for a whole lamb, “…they are to share with the nearest neighbor based on the number of people…” So the lamb gets divided according to how many are eating. I think that makes for a very friendly night.
No altar in this one, friend. The LORD says the blood goes “…on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs.” The doorframes are the spot, not an altar.
That's a creative guess, baker, but earlobes aren't in this one. The LORD says the blood goes on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs. Doorframes, not earlobes.

Secret isn't the word, baker. The LORD says, “You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD’s Passover.” The word He gives is haste. And the meal gets its name right there in the same line: the LORD’s Passover.

You've got it, baker. The LORD says, “…on this very day I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt.” That's His reason for the feast. He adds, “You must keep this day as a permanent statute for the generations to come.”
No sign is requested here, friend. The text says, “Then the people bowed down and worshiped.” A sign isn't mentioned. What the text shows them doing is bowing and worshiping.

Yes, baker. The text says, “And the Israelites went and did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.” Moses was Israel's leader, and Aaron was his brother (Exodus 4:14). The people did what was commanded. But the story isn't over yet, so there's more still to come.

It's actually true, friend. The text says, “And the Israelites went and did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.” Moses was Israel's leader, and Aaron was his brother (Exodus 4:14). The people did what the LORD commanded. And the story isn't over, so there's more still to come.
